work.title: Passions-Cantata som i Fasten opføres af det musikalske Selskab
Vor Harpe er bleven til Sorrig
Passionskantate 'Vor Harpe er bleven til Sorrig'

history.p: In 1768, Scheibe asked the young up-coming poet Johannes Ewald, with whom he had collaborated regarding the funeral cantata for Frederik VI two years earlier (SchW B2:415), if he would write a new text to which Scheibe would compose the music. Apparently Scheibe considered using the music which he had composed for the funeral cantata; however, a comparison between the two works reveals that only eight of the nineteen movements were reused. Ewald comments on the fruitful collaboration, which was even noticed by contemporaries such as the poet Edvard Storm. Ewald mentions having received lessons from Scheibe: ‘For me, he was a father and it is certain that if there is anything in my poetic work, which in purpose as to music may deserve applause, then I have only to thank the instructive relationship with him and his loving lessons.’ The Passion cantata received its first performance during Lent 1768 and was repeated several times during Scheibe’s lifetime and was even performed by the musical society in Bergen, Norway, in 1770 and 1809. Presumably Claus Fasting, who studied in Copenhagen and may have heard the first performance of the cantata, brought the work to Bergen. Besides Scheibe’s autograph ink fair copy, also a transcription, presumably produced sometime around 1774‒76, has survived. It was at that time that the cantata was performed at Det kongelige musikalske Akademi. The transcription ‒ which once belonged to Ludvig Fabritius Tengnagel who might have inherited it from his father, a great promoter of music and a member of the musical academy ‒ is not entirely identical to the autograph. It includes, for example, a duet for a 'faithful soul' and an 'angel' and a choir section. The sections which are only referred to in the autograph score ('Duetto & Coro') are based on a movement from another popular Passion cantata composed in 1762 (SchW B2:302). Furthermore the trumpets and kettledrum which are ad libitum in the autograph score are left out in the transcript, except the ‘Duetto & Coro’ section. It is doubtful whether either Scheibe or Ewald considered the two extra movements as part of the work; they were probably added due to requests (singers, audience).

incipText.p: Vor Harpe er bleven til Sorrig
I Kedrons stille Dale
Guds Vredes Straaler brænder over Horeb
Græde I, som boe paa Jorden!
Jeg seer Ham. – Gud! – og denne er min Skaber!
Hvo kan bestaae for en almægtig Vrede
Forhænget revner, og en hellig Flamme igiennemtrænger det rædsomme Mørke
O stille Skræk! – Guds Rædsel! – Hiertet standser
De skal udbrede din store Godheds Ihukommelse
Han fandtes ene værdig, at agtes for retfærdig
Jeg saae: og Mørkets grumme Kiæmpe igiennemløb et forvirret Øye
Slaae Cithar, slaae i sagte Toner
Langt under Chaos er de mørke Huuler
O Graad, du Glædens tause Tolk
Men Himlen taug, – Seraphen selv holdt inde
Lad Himlene fornemme
Stor var Han – fød af Evigheders Fader
Naar Himle flye din Røst, naar Verdner skiule sig
Bliv Taare ved at trille
Triumpf? Men, ak! den dyrekiøbes

physDesc.watermark: At least two distinct watermarks are seen of which one is Dutch: 1) end flyleaf and front paste-down: ‘P. VALET | FIN | PERIGORD | 1742’ and the coat-of-arms of Amsterdam set between two lions (cf. Heawood:407 (342−438)); 2) the Pro Patria emblem (a fence surrounding a lion with a sword, a woman holding a pole with a hat on top, and between pole and the woman’s head the letters WW; cf. Heawood:3704); 3) a coat-of-arms with the lettering ‘CIK’ (?) on top.
physDesc.physMedium: In 2o; upright format consisting of folded and nested bifolios; front flyleaf, title page (fol. 1r), blank page (fol. 1v), music (fols. 2r–69v; numbered 1–138), end flyleaf; in all 138 pages. Hand-ruled paper with 20 staves (8 mm; single rastrum used) in brown ink and music in black ink; pp. 27–30 have an added stave in black ink (same rastrum). Score contains numerous autograph changes, cancellations, and corrections in ink and should be termed a working copy; some bar numbers have been added in pencil, presumably during the production of a new full score in the 1940s (‘Egne Afskrifter’).
In original half-binding with leather spine and corners and brownish marbled paper; paper of a fairly good quality.

titlePage.label: Title (upper board)
titlePage.p: Passions Cantata | componeret af | Capelmester J: A: Scheibe.

physDesc.watermark: a crowned coat-of-arms with a fleur-de-lis, at the bottom ‘4+’ with ‘WR’ appended (cf. Heawood:1805, 1806; and dated to before 1722).
physDesc.physMedium: In 2o; upright format; no flyleaves, no title page, music (fols. 1r−106v; numbered 1−212, a few numbers in pencil otherwise in ink); in all 212 pages; a page between 210 and 211 has been removed perhaps due to errors or as a cancellation. Hand-ruled paper with 14 staves (10 mm; single rastrum used) in brown ink and music in same ink; from p. 81 however the music has been written in black and very dark brown ink; pp. 27−32 have an extra stave added in black ink (same rastrum). The front paste-down has ‘L.F. de Tengnagel’ added in ink. The score is a clean copy with only very changes in pencil, some changes in ink, and shows very little wear. Surprisingly the paper seems to be from before 1750. Ludvig Fabritius de Tengnagel (born c. 1819) who apparently owned this transcript was a musician and an amateur composer and may have used it for his work with his own Oratorio (beginning of the nineteenth century). It seems most likely that the transcript is contemporary with Scheibe. It contains an extra movement, 'Duetto & Coro', which only is referred to in the autograph score. The source, which was probably based on Scheibe's autograph score, was most likely produced sometime around 1774 when the extra section 'Duetto & Coro' was added and included in the second edition of the printed text (Thiele, DK-Kk, M 19693 8o).
Original half-binding with leather spine and corners, marbled paper, and label on front cover; paper of a fairly dense quality.

physDesc.physMedium: In 8o; title page (sig. [*1r]; p. [1]), blank page (sig. [*1v]; p. [2]), text (pp. [3]–16); in all 16 pages. Publication has not been dated; however, based on the facts that a royal privilege was given to the musical academy on 10 August 1774 (though existing already in January that year) and that the printer, Johan Rudolph Thiele, bought his workshop in 1770, it seems likely that the libretto was published sometime during 1774–76. It is the earliest edition which includes the extra Duetto and Coro section. The text has been reset and modernised.
Originally in limp binding of marbled paper, now in modern library binding with shelf marks in pencil on front paste-down.

physDesc.physMedium: In 8o; front flyleaf, frontispiece with a portrait of Ewald ('Clemens del: et Sculp:'), title page (sig. [a1r]); p. [i]), blank page (sig. [a1v]; p. [ii]), 'to the reader' (pp. [iii]–xxxix), list of subscribers (pp. [xl]–lxvi), table of contents (sig. e2r–v), text (pp. [1]–456), end flyleaf; in all 504 pages. The text does not include Scheibe's Duetto and Coro section as the earlier libretto (c. 1774–76) did, implying that Ewald did not consider it as part of the work though it appears in a later libretto (1784). Text, which has been gently modernised, appears on pp. 235–46.
Paper of a good quality. Full-bound in leather with red title label in gold lettering on spine and green label in gold lettering indicating volume.
